title: A neighborhood gathering place can be followed by more local startups where comparable social venues were absent
source_unit: U.S. census tract and business-registration comparison in NBER Working Paper 32604 using the Startup Cartography Project
geography: United States census tracts; neighborhoods without existing coffee shops at the comparison baseline

observations.period: 1990–2022 business-registration data; seven years after Starbucks entry

denominator.unit: U.S. census tracts scheduled to receive a Starbucks compared with tracts that did not receive the planned café; exact analytical count not stated in the public abstract

startup_change.value: 9.1%–22.5% increase, or about 2.9–6.4 additional firms per year
startup_change.unit: reported difference in annual startup count over the seven years after entry

under_resourced_partnership.value: the Starbucks–Magic Johnson partnership in underprivileged neighborhoods produced larger effects

existing_cafe_counterexample.value: no significant entrepreneurship effect where cafés already existed

mechanism.value: analyses suggest networks are part of the pathway

durable_firm_or_household_welfare.unit: missing firm survival, jobs, wages, owner income, customer prices, displacement, housing, and household outcomes

observations.method: Comparison of business-registration outcomes in census tracts receiving a first Starbucks with tracts scheduled to receive one but not receiving it, using Startup Cartography Project data; the public abstract reports estimated startup differences and mechanism analyses.
observations.uncertainty: The public abstract does not expose the full sample, exact treatment-selection process, all effect sizes, standard errors, or firm-level survival and quality outcomes. Startup formation is a local economic indicator, not proof that the new firms survived or improved resident welfare.
observations.subgroup: Census tracts without existing coffee shops, with separate attention to under-resourced neighborhoods and tracts where cafés already existed; neighborhood and founder-level distributions are not fully reported in the abstract.
observations.counterinterpretation: Starbucks entry may signal expected growth or bring customers and foot traffic rather than create networks directly; the null effect where cafés already exist supports a missing-third-place interpretation but does not prove a single mechanism.

related_sources.claim: NBER's summary reports localized startup increases, larger effects in an under-resourced-neighborhood partnership, no significant effect where cafés already existed, and distance patterns consistent with a network mechanism.

boundary: This record adds a place-linked firm-formation result and an important counterexample: a new gathering venue was associated with more startups where comparable cafés were absent, while entry did not show the same effect where cafés already existed. It does not establish firm survival, job quality, customer welfare, housing affordability, displacement, or individual social connection.
